Maladaptive Strategies.value: Situations that put my body under stress
I clean or organise things repeatedly to feel in control
Going out at night or being outside after dark

issues.item: Avoid Dreams: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares
issues.explanation: These three maladaptive strategy items do not form a clinically coherent set on their own. 'Avoid Dreams' and 'Avoid Physical Stress' are trauma-linked avoidance strategies, but 'Compulsive Cleaning' reflects a distinct control/ritualising pattern that is not clearly tied to the same military PTSD presentation in the absence of any supporting trigger, threat, memory, or appraisal items. With no active edges in the formulation, the node should still be internally coherent; here the items suggest different mechanisms (nightmare avoidance, bodily arousal avoidance, and compulsive control rituals) without evidence they belong to the same symptom pattern.

vignette: Zahra is a 21-year-old Middle Eastern woman who works as a Database Administrator. She has sought help for symptoms that have been significantly impacting her life since her traumatic experience during military service two years ago. Zahra’s trauma involved an IED explosion while on patrol, which resulted in multiple casualties and left her with lasting psychological scars. Zahra vividly recalls the intense physical stress she endured that day—feeling like her body was under constant threat as she tried to assist those around her. Since then, she has become highly sensitive to situations where her body feels taxed or exposed to danger. For instance, even a short jog at the gym triggers flashbacks of that explosive event and leaves her feeling overwhelmed. As a result, Zahra now avoids any activity that could put her body under stress, such as outdoor running or intense workouts. This avoidance has had practical consequences in her daily life. Zahra’s work environment requires occasional late-night shifts to ensure database security, but she finds these shifts particularly challenging. The darkness and quiet of the night remind her of the eerie silence after the explosion, which often leaves her feeling unsafe and anxious. She tries to organize her tasks so that they are completed before dark, even if it means working longer hours in daylight. To maintain a sense of control over her environment, Zahra has also developed compulsive cleaning habits at home and work. The meticulous organization and cleanliness provide her with a semblance of order amidst the chaos she feels internally. She spends excessive time arranging items and sanitizing surfaces to ensure everything is perfect, which can take up hours each day. This behavior has become a coping mechanism that helps her feel secure and in control. Despite these strategies, Zahra’s symptoms have progressively worsened over time. The avoidance of physical stress and nighttime activities has led to an increasingly isolated lifestyle. She finds herself withdrawing from social gatherings and spending more time alone at home, further exacerbating feelings of loneliness and disconnection. Her compulsive cleaning rituals, while initially helpful, now consume much of her free time and interfere with other aspects of her life. What finally brought Zahra to seek help was a realization that she could no longer sustain this lifestyle without significant personal costs. She is most afraid of losing her job due to the constraints her behaviors impose on her work schedule, as well as the growing sense of isolation from friends and family. However, she also hopes for a way to reclaim control over her life without these debilitating coping mechanisms. Zahra’s fears are rooted in her deep-seated belief that any form of physical stress or exposure to nighttime darkness will inevitably trigger traumatic memories and overwhelming anxiety. This cycle has become increasingly difficult to manage on her own, leading her to recognize the need for professional support to navigate these challenges effectively.
